items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a rise in sea level above the normal tide caused by low pressure and strong onshore winds”.
items.answer: Storm surge
items.markingKey: Storm surge: a rise in sea level above the normal tide caused by low pressure and strong onshore winds. [1]

items.stem: Explain the global distribution of tropical cyclones.
items.answer: Over warm oceans (above 26.5 °C) between about 5° and 20-30° N and S; not at the equator (no Coriolis effect) or in the South Atlantic and SE Pacific (cold water, wind shear); most in the NW Pacific.

items.stem: Explain the hazards associated with tropical cyclones.
items.answer: High winds damage buildings and crops; storm surges flood coasts; torrential rain causes river floods and landslides; tornadoes may form; secondary hazards include disease and contamination of water.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per hazard [4]

items.stem: A tropical cyclone approaching the coast of Bangladesh has a central pressure of 918 hPa (normal pressure 1013 hPa). Each 1 hPa fall in pressure raises sea level by about 1 cm. Onshore winds are forecast to add a further 3.1 m, and landfall coincides with a high tide 1.8 m above mean sea level. The track shows the centre moved 110 km in the last 6 hours. Much of the coastal land lies 5.1 m above mean sea level. (a) Calculate the forward speed of the cyclone. (b) Explain why the shape of the coastline affects storm surge height.
items.answer: (a) 18.3 km/h (b) Shallow, gently sloping continental shelves and funnel-shaped bays concentrate water, so surges are higher (Bay of Bengal); steep, deep coasts have smaller surges.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that storm surge is the most dangerous hazard associated with tropical cyclones? In your answer you may refer to wind, vulnerability and rainfall.
items.answer: For: Surges cause most deaths in low-lying coasts and deltas (Bhola 1970, Nargis 2008, Haiyan 2013, Katrina 2005). Against: Rain-induced flooding and landslides cause most deaths inland and in mountainous islands (Mitch 1998 in Honduras, Harvey 2017); wind destroys buildings and crops. Conclusion: Surge is usually the deadliest hazard on low coasts, but the main hazard varies with relief, storm speed and vulnerability.

items.stem: Explain why storm surges are particularly dangerous in places such as Bangladesh.
items.answer: The shallow, funnel-shaped Bay of Bengal amplifies surges; the delta is very low-lying and densely populated; many people are poor with weak housing (1970 Bhola, 1991).

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a violently rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm cloud to the ground”.
items.answer: Tornado
items.markingKey: Tornado: a violently rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm cloud to the ground. [1]

items.stem: Explain how tornadoes form.
items.answer: Warm, moist air at low levels and cold, dry air above give instability; wind shear makes the updraft rotate, forming a mesocyclone in a supercell; downdrafts and stretching concentrate the rotation into a narrow vortex reaching the ground.

items.stem: Explain why tornadoes are difficult to predict.
items.answer: They are small and short-lived and form within storms; conditions favourable for tornadoes can be forecast hours ahead, but individual tornadoes are usually detected by Doppler radar only minutes before they strike.

items.stem: “Tornadoes are a greater hazard to people than tropical cyclones.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to warning time, vulnerability and wind speed.
items.answer: For: Tornadoes have the strongest surface winds, strike with little warning and destroy everything in their path (Joplin 2011, Moore 2013). Against: Tropical cyclones affect much larger areas for longer, with storm surge and floods causing far more deaths and damage (Haiyan, Katrina, Nargis). Conclusion: Locally tornadoes are more intense, but tropical cyclones are the greater hazard to people overall.

items.stem: Compare the hazards of tornadoes and tropical cyclones.
items.answer: Tornadoes have faster winds (over 320 km/h) but narrow paths and short duration; cyclones affect areas hundreds of km wide for days with surge and flooding, so total damage and deaths are usually larger.

items.stem: Explain how tropical cyclones are predicted.
items.answer: Satellites track cloud systems; hurricane-hunter aircraft and buoys measure pressure and winds; computer models forecast track and intensity; forecasts are shown as cones of uncertainty with warnings issued 36-48 hours ahead.

items.stem: Explain why the impacts of tropical cyclones differ between HICs and LICs.
items.answer: HICs have better forecasts, communications, building codes, evacuation and insurance, so fewer deaths but higher economic losses; LICs have more vulnerable housing, poverty and weak infrastructure, so more deaths (Katrina vs Nargis).

items.answer: Error increases with lead time, from 84 km at 24 h to 212 km at 72 h, about 2.5 times larger.

items.stem: Table 11.3 shows mean track forecast errors (km) for Atlantic hurricanes at a forecasting centre. 1992: 24 h 181, 48 h 338, 72 h 473. 2023: 24 h 52, 48 h 111, 72 h 136. (a) Describe how forecast error changes with lead time in 2023. (b) Explain why reduced forecast errors save lives and money.
items.answer: (a) Error increases with lead time, from 52 km at 24 h to 136 km at 72 h, about 2.6 times larger. (b) Warning areas can be smaller and more accurate, so evacuations are better targeted and trusted, fewer people are evacuated unnecessarily and more time is available to prepare.

items.stem: Assess the view that improvements in prediction have been the main reason for the fall in deaths from tropical cyclones.
items.answer: For: Satellites and models reduced track errors and allow evacuation days ahead; Bangladesh warnings in 2007 (Sidr) and 2020 (Amphan) contrasted with 1970. Against: Shelters, education, building codes, evacuation planning, community volunteers and development (better housing, communications) were essential; warnings in Myanmar 2008 failed to reach people. Conclusion: Prediction is necessary but not sufficient; falling deaths come from prediction combined with preparedness and reduced vulnerability.

items.answer: Not correct. Warnings must reach people, be trusted and acted on, as Katrina and Nargis showed.

items.stem: Explain why forecasts of intensity are less accurate than forecasts of track.
items.answer: Intensity depends on small-scale processes in the eyewall, ocean heat below the surface and wind shear that models represent poorly; rapid intensification is hard to predict.

items.stem: Table 11.3 shows mean track forecast errors (km) for Atlantic hurricanes at a forecasting centre. 1995: 24 h 169, 48 h 353, 72 h 508. 2022: 24 h 70, 48 h 127, 72 h 186. (a) Explain why forecasts have improved. (b) Explain why reduced forecast errors save lives and money.
items.answer: (a) More and better satellite data, aircraft reconnaissance, faster computers running higher-resolution models, ensemble forecasting and better understanding of steering winds. items.stem: To what extent do you agree that tornadoes are a greater hazard to people than tropical cyclones? In your answer you may refer to wind speed and area affected.
items.answer: For: Tornadoes have the strongest surface winds, strike with little warning and destroy everything in their path (Joplin 2011, Moore 2013). Against: Tropical cyclones affect much larger areas for longer, with storm surge and floods causing far more deaths and damage (Haiyan, Katrina, Nargis). Conclusion: Locally tornadoes are more intense, but tropical cyclones are the greater hazard to people overall.

items.stem: “Improvements in prediction have been the main reason for the fall in deaths from tropical cyclones.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to shelters, development and education.
items.answer: For: Satellites and models reduced track errors and allow evacuation days ahead; Bangladesh warnings in 2007 (Sidr) and 2020 (Amphan) contrasted with 1970. Against: Shelters, education, building codes, evacuation planning, community volunteers and development (better housing, communications) were essential; warnings in Myanmar 2008 failed to reach people. Conclusion: Prediction is necessary but not sufficient; falling deaths come from prediction combined with preparedness and reduced vulnerability.

items.stem: A tropical cyclone approaching the Mississippi delta, USA has a central pressure of 940 hPa (normal pressure 1013 hPa). Each 1 hPa fall in pressure raises sea level by about 1 cm. Onshore winds are forecast to add a further 3.7 m, and landfall coincides with a high tide 1.4 m above mean sea level. The track shows the centre moved 112 km in the last 6 hours. Much of the coastal land lies 2.9 m above mean sea level. Explain why the shape of the coastline affects storm surge height.
items.answer: Shallow, gently sloping continental shelves and funnel-shaped bays concentrate water, so surges are higher (Bay of Bengal); steep, deep coasts have smaller surges.

items.stem: “Storm surge is the most dangerous hazard associated with tropical cyclones.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to rainfall and wind.
items.answer: For: Surges cause most deaths in low-lying coasts and deltas (Bhola 1970, Nargis 2008, Haiyan 2013, Katrina 2005). Against: Rain-induced flooding and landslides cause most deaths inland and in mountainous islands (Mitch 1998 in Honduras, Harvey 2017); wind destroys buildings and crops. Conclusion: Surge is usually the deadliest hazard on low coasts, but the main hazard varies with relief, storm speed and vulnerability.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how tornadoes form. (b) Compare the hazards of tornadoes and tropical cyclones.
items.answer: (a) Warm, moist air at low levels and cold, dry air above give instability; wind shear makes the updraft rotate, forming a mesocyclone in a supercell; downdrafts and stretching concentrate the rotation into a narrow vortex reaching the ground. (b) Tornadoes have faster winds (over 320 km/h) but narrow paths and short duration; cyclones affect areas hundreds of km wide for days with surge and flooding, so total damage and deaths are usually larger.
